name: Lonapegsomatropin

lead: Lonapegsomatropin (Skytrofa) is a once-weekly growth hormone injection approved by the FDA in 2021 for children and adults with growth hormone deficiency. It is mentioned in height-focused circles because GH drives growth velocity.

It is a pegylated prodrug that releases somatropin, which binds the GH receptor and acts partly through IGF-1. Phase 3 trials compared it with daily somatropin in treatment-naive and switched children. All trials involve people with a diagnosed deficiency; none tests it for height in people without one.

paras: It is prescribed as a weekly injection for children aged 1 and older weighing at least 11.5 kg, and for adults with GH deficiency, replacing daily GH.
The label lists warnings including neoplasm risk, glucose intolerance, intracranial hypertension, fluid retention, hypoadrenalism, hypothyroidism and hypersensitivity. It is prescription-only.

angle.text: Lonapegsomatropin is a weekly prescription GH prodrug that raises growth in children and adults with diagnosed deficiency, so it appears in height-focused circles. Its trials involve people with GH deficiency.

lead: Lonapegsomatropin (brand name Skytrofa; development name TransCon hGH) is a once-weekly, long-acting prodrug of growth hormone given by subcutaneous injection. The US FDA approved it in August 2021 for pediatric growth hormone deficiency (GHD) [1][2].

The US label covers children aged 1 year and older weighing at least 11.5 kg with growth failure due to inadequate endogenous GH secretion, and adults with GHD [3]. Phase 3 trials compared it with daily somatropin in treatment-naive and switched children [4][5].
It is a prescription medicine for diagnosed deficiency. No trial has tested it for height or appearance in people without a deficiency.

paras: The US label lists pediatric patients aged 1 year and older weighing at least 11.5 kg with growth failure from inadequate GH secretion, and replacement of GH in adults with GHD [3]. Trials are registered in Turner syndrome, in short stature from GH-sufficient disorders such as idiopathic short stature and small-for-gestational-age, and in achondroplasia [6][7][8].

The label describes it as a pegylated human growth hormone (somatropin) that binds the GH receptor, with direct tissue and metabolic effects and indirect effects through IGF-1, including stimulation of chondrocyte differentiation and proliferation [3]. A modelling paper describes predicting average IGF-1 levels with once-weekly dosing [9].

The US labels for long-acting growth hormones list warnings including increased mortality in acute critical illness, severe hypersensitivity, increased risk of neoplasms (notably second neoplasms in childhood cancer survivors), glucose intolerance and diabetes mellitus, intracranial hypertension, fluid retention, hypoadrenalism and hypothyroidism [3]. Label pregnancy information notes no available human data for this drug, that decades of published somatropin data have not identified a pregnancy risk, and that rat studies showed no embryo-fetal harm [3].

The phase 3 heiGHt trial compared weekly lonapegsomatropin with daily somatropin in treatment-naive children with GHD [4]. The fliGHt trial examined switching from daily somatropin [5], and the enliGHten extension reported two-year safety and efficacy [10]. Adult phase 3 trials, including a placebo and daily-somatropin comparison, have completed [11][12]. Reviews and a network meta-analysis compare it with other long-acting products [13][14][15]. Post-authorisation safety studies are registered [16][17].
